name: french beef and mushroom stew
instructions:
TWO VARIANTS. Both land on the same herb axis (rosemary + thyme + bay leaf), same acid (red wine — not cabernet), and the same umami-boost stack (tomato paste + worcestershire + cholula hot sauce). They're close to identical on ingredient adds — kept as separate variants because I anticipate future divergence (e.g., variant B leaning harder on the porcini + nutritional yeast umami stack; variant A staying purer to Julia's classical shape).

=== VARIANT A — JULIA CHILD'S BOEUF BOURGUIGNON (WITH MY ADDITIONS) ===

Julia Child's canonical boeuf bourguignon from Mastering the Art of French Cooking, Vol. 1 — WITH my additions of rosemary, cholula hot sauce, and worcestershire sauce alongside her thyme + bay leaf. The rosemary is the biggest departure from Julia's original.

INGREDIENTS (per Julia, plus my adds):
- 6 oz chunk of bacon (rind removed and blanched separately; the bacon cut into lardons)
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 3 lb lean stewing beef (chuck), cut into 2-inch cubes
- 1 carrot, sliced
- 1 white onion, sliced (Julia calls for yellow; I use white per this cookbook's white-onion rule)
- salt + freshly ground black pepper
- 2 tbsp all-purpose flour
- 3 cups full-bodied young red wine (Burgundy / Chianti / Côtes-du-Rhône) — NOT cabernet, see notes
- 2-3 cups brown beef stock (enough to just cover)
- 1 tbsp tomato paste
- 2 cloves garlic, mashed
- 1/2 tsp thyme
- 1 bay leaf, crumbled
- blanched bacon rind (from the chunk of bacon)
- 18-24 pearl onions, braised separately in stock with a bouquet garni
- 1 lb fresh mushrooms, quartered, sautéed hard separately in butter
- MY ADDITIONS: fresh rosemary (in the braise), a few dashes of cholula hot sauce, a splash of worcestershire

PROCEDURE:
1. Simmer bacon rind + lardons in water for 10 min. Drain and pat dry.
2. Sauté lardons in olive oil in a heavy casserole; remove.
3. Brown the beef cubes in the same fat, in batches — real color, don't crowd. Remove.
4. Cook the sliced carrot + onion in the same fat until softened.
5. Return the beef + bacon to the casserole. Sprinkle with salt, pepper, and the 2 tbsp flour; toss to coat.
6. Uncovered in a 450°F oven for 4 min. Toss. Back in for 4 min more. (This browns the flour with the meat — Julia's specific step.) Reduce oven to 325°F.
7. Pour in wine + enough beef stock to just cover the meat. Stir in tomato paste, mashed garlic, thyme, bay leaf, and the blanched bacon rind. Add MY ADDITIONS: rosemary, worcestershire, cholula.
8. Bring to a simmer on the stovetop, cover, and braise in the 325°F oven for 3-4 hours (until fork-tender).
9. MEANWHILE: braise pearl onions (brown in butter, then finish in stock with a bouquet garni). Sauté quartered mushrooms hard in butter — don't crowd the pan.
10. Combine the braise + pearl onions + mushrooms at the end. Fish out the bay leaf and bacon rind. Taste; adjust salt, pepper, hot sauce.

No potatoes in Julia's canonical (see notes on potatoes — that's a variant B feature).

=== VARIANT B — VEGETARIAN (VEGAN MEAT + BUTTER BASE) ===

Structurally the current cookbook's beef-and-mushroom stew, built on ground vegan beef (Abbott's / soy beef crumbles) OR impossible/beyond formed into MEATBALLS (pre-baked, see notes). Fat base is BUTTER (main) — which makes this a VEGETARIAN dish, not vegan, even when the meat itself is vegan.

INGREDIENTS:
- BUTTER (main fat) + olive oil (supporting)
- ground vegan beef (Abbott's / soy beef crumbles) OR impossible/beyond meatballs (pre-baked; see IMPOSSIBLE/BEYOND note in the shared notes)
- white onions, coarse chopped
- carrots, coarse chopped
- parsnips (optional, coarse chopped)
- garlic, mashed
- mushrooms (portabella / oyster / shittake — any or all), coarse chopped
- potatoes, coarse chopped ~1-inch chunks (LOAD-BEARING — see POTATOES ARE CRITICAL note)
- red wine (pinot noir / burgundy / syrah / malbec — NOT cabernet)
- bouillon or real vegetable/vegan-beef stock
- tomato paste
- fresh tomato, chopped (extra tomato flavor — see TOMATO note)
- rosemary, thyme, bay leaf (mandatory pair rosemary + bay leaf dominant; thyme supporting)
- worcestershire sauce (or vegan worcestershire if going fully vegan)
- cholula hot sauce
- red chili flakes
- nutritional yeast (secondary — part of the umami stack)
- porcini mushroom powder (secondary — reinforces mushroom depth)
- all-purpose flour (for the roux)
- salt + black pepper

PROCEDURE:
1. Sauté the mushrooms hard in butter first. This is the roux fond.
2. Whisk in flour for a roux (blond → light brown).
3. Add the coarse-chopped onions, carrots, garlic. DEEP SAUTÉ for real caramelization — don't rush this stage (see COARSE CHOP + DEEP SAUTÉ note).
4. Add wine + stock. Add potatoes, tomato paste, chopped fresh tomato, worcestershire, cholula, red chili flakes.
5. Add rosemary, thyme, bay leaf.
6. Add the vegan meat late in the braise: ground vegan beef stirred in, or pre-baked impossible/beyond meatballs nestled in.
7. Stir in nutritional yeast + porcini mushroom powder — small amounts, part of a broader stack.
8. Simmer until potatoes are tender and the stew has thickened. Fish out bay leaf.

See notes for shared rules (deep sauté, no fresh herbs, wine rules, fridge-aging behavior) and technique-specific callouts (pre-baking impossible meatballs, why potatoes are load-bearing here but not in variant A).

NOTE: a pure-vegetable variant was drafted here (celery root/turnips + no tomato + ginger/turmeric herbs + white wine) and rejected — didn't work well. That set of ideas moved to french-onion-vegetable-soup as its broader-vegetable variant, which is the right home for it.
notes:
French beef and mushroom stew — a bourguignon-shaped dish where beef and mushrooms are co-equal primaries, not a substitution of one for the other. REAL CHUNKS OF BEEF (chuck or similar stew cut) are the default. For a vegan version, GROUND vegan beef is the substitute — see the meat note below on why ground vegan beats chunky seitan here. The mushrooms aren't standing in for anything — they're the second headliner alongside the beef.

TECHNIQUE: start with sauteed mushrooms in butter, then flour for roux. Other vegetables like celery/carrot are stew vegetables coarsely chopped, not sauce base (finely chopped and sauteed).

COARSE CHOP + DEEP SAUTÉ (NO MIREPOIX): coarse-chop the onions, carrots, celery, and mushrooms into visible chunks — same rule as coq au vin, this is a rustic stew and you want to see and taste discrete vegetable pieces in the finished dish, not a dissolved-into-sauce mirepoix base. That said, sauté them HARD enough to get real caramelization on the surfaces before the wine and stock go in. The deep-sauté / maillard phase does structural flavor work that a rushed softening step doesn't provide. Rush the sauté and the finished stew reads flat.

CELERY IS A RESCUE INGREDIENT — SECONDARY, WITH A MEDITERRANEAN COST: celery isn't primary here, but it's an unusually useful correction step when the dish has gone off balance. If you dumped in too much tomato paste, over-poured the red wine, or otherwise let one axis dominate, adding coarsely-chopped celery to the braise pulls the flavors back toward center — its neutral savory-vegetal character absorbs excess tang and mellows the dish. THE COST: celery drags the stew's register toward mediterranean-vegetable-soup / minestrone territory, which is exactly the direction the rosemary + bay + tomato axis is trying to escape. So use celery when you need to rescue a batch, but know that a rescued stew reads slightly more italian and less french-classical than a properly-balanced one. If you're using celery from the start (rather than as a fix), keep the quantity modest — a stalk or two, coarse chop, not a full mirepoix.

POTATOES ARE CRITICAL — VARIANT B ONLY, LOAD-BEARING THERE: potatoes are load-bearing IN VARIANT B (the vegetarian version). They give the stew its starchy, hearty body and absorb the tomato-and-wine sauce properly. Coarse-chop into ~1-inch chunks; add during the braise. VARIANT A (Julia's classical) has NO potatoes — Julia's original doesn't use them, and the pearl-onion + separate-mushroom-sauté structure carries the dish without a starch component. Don't add potatoes to variant A; don't skip them in variant B. This is a MAJOR DIFFERENTIATOR from coq au vin (see coq-au-vin), which has NO potatoes and would be ruined by them — variant B's tomato + worcestershire umami structure holds up to the starch absorption; coq au vin's delicate pinot noir base would be dulled and diluted.

MEAT — VARIANT A USES REAL BEEF CHUNKS; VARIANT B USES VEGAN MEAT (WITH BUTTER BASE = VEGETARIAN):
- VARIANT A — REAL BEEF (CHUNKS): chuck (or similar stew-cut beef) cut into 2-inch cubes per Julia. The chunks carry the umami and texture the long braise needs; connective tissue breaks down over the cook to enrich the sauce.
- VARIANT B — GROUND VEGAN BEEF (ABBOTT'S / SOY BEEF CRUMBLES): the canonical variant B meat. Ground vegan beef works better here than chunky seitan — seitan chunks don't render or break down like real beef chuck does; they stay rubbery. Ground vegan beef distributes through the dish and picks up the braise. NOTE: variant B uses BUTTER as the fat base (not bacon lardons like variant A), which makes the dish VEGETARIAN even when using vegan meat — not vegan.
- VARIANT B ALTERNATE — IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND BEEF AS MEATBALLS: usable in variant B when formed into MEATBALLS (see IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND note below on why meatballs, not crumbles, and the pre-bake step). Distinctly flavored, so use judgment.
- SOY CURLS: untested (see want_to_try). Curious whether they'd behave more like real beef chunks than seitan does.
Flavor in variant B is NOT derived from the meat itself; a good vegan beef bouillon or vegetable stock is doing the heavy lifting.

HERBS / AROMATICS (non-optional): rosemary and bay leaf in large quantities are mandatory — this pair should DOMINATE the herb axis. Rosemary is nice-to-have in chicken stews or italian vegetable soups, but it's mandatory here — the wine + soy meat + potatoes + mushrooms + carrots will be flat without the sharpness of bay leaf and rosemary together. Thyme can go alongside rosemary (welcome supporting herb) but rosemary + bay leaf should stay the dominant pair; thyme in a supporting role, not co-lead. Garlic is also non-optional. Use sharp white onions, not yellow or red.

ROSEMARY IS RIGHT HERE, WRONG IN COQ AU VIN (SEE COQ-AU-VIN): the coq au vin recipe explicitly clashes rosemary — its pinot-noir-and-chicken register is too delicate and rosemary overpowers. This beef variant is the opposite: the wine is bigger (see wine note below), the meat is richer, and rosemary is what pulls it together. The two dishes are structurally opposed on this axis. Don't backport thyme+sage from coq au vin here (too subtle) and don't backport rosemary to coq au vin (too aggressive).

WINE — NOT CABERNET (SAME RULE AS COQ AU VIN): cabernet's tannins and fruit-forward jamminess can ruin this dish too, even though the beef and tomato structure is more forgiving than coq au vin's. A cabernet ends up dominating the sauce and pushing the flavor toward a red-wine-reduction rather than a stew. A traditional burgundy or pinot noir works; a syrah or malbec is fine here (unlike coq au vin) because the beef and tomato paste can hold up to a bigger red. Just not cabernet.

NORTHERN PULL: worcestershire sauce rounds it out and pushes the flavor more 'northern'. Without it the rosemary/bay/tomato combination can drift italian even with the potatoes.

=== BOUILLON / STOCK — BEEF-FLAVORED IS BEST ===

For this stew (both variants), beef-flavored bouillon or stock is best. Reach for BETTER THAN BOUILLON'S BEEF BASE if you're using a concentrated bouillon paste; real beef stock if you have it. This is the OPPOSITE of what works in french-onion-vegetable-soup, where dark vegetable bouillon works better than beef base — the beef stew register wants the beef flavor for real, not just savory-hearty depth.

=== NEVER FRESH HERBS OR FRESH GREENS — HARD RULE, LEARNED EARLY ===

A lesson learned early on: FRESH HERBS (parsley, tarragon) and FRESH GREENS (spinach, mixed greens) are a hard 'never' for this recipe. Not 'use sparingly' or 'as a garnish' — actually leave them out. Where they belong instead:
- FRESH HERBS (parsley, tarragon) → save for french chicken stews (see french-chicken-soup, chicken-with-vinegar) where they carry the herb axis properly. This recipe's herb axis is rosemary + bay leaf (dominant), thyme (supporting) — dried and cooked into the braise. Fresh finishing herbs fight that structure.
- FRESH GREENS (spinach, mixed greens) → save for earthy italian tomato soups (see italian-minestrone-soup family) where they slot in cleanly, or use as a side salad alongside this stew.

Tarragon was previously in the primary ingredient list here — moved to clashing to reflect the actual rule. Parsley, spinach, mixed greens already were clashing; this note extends the 'why.'

=== NO FENNEL BULB — DOESN'T WORK HERE ===

Fennel bulb used to live in the primary ingredient list; removed. It doesn't really work in this stew. Save fennel bulb for french-onion-vegetable-soup or for ratatouille-shaped dishes that don't contain gravy elements.

=== NO PARSNIPS — TOO SWEET FOR THE BEEF VERSION ===

Parsnips are too sweet for this stew. Tomato + red wine + parsnips stacks up as a lot of fruity — three fruit-adjacent notes fighting each other. Reach for carrots (and celery in a pinch) instead. Parsnips are a want-to-try over in french-onion-vegetable-soup variant B where the pure-vegetable register can absorb them.

TOMATO: use more tomato paste than traditional boeuf bourguignon, and add a chopped fresh tomato as extra tomato flavor — you get less umami from the pseudo meat than from real beef, so compensate here. Tomatoes are non-optional for this recipe.

FAT BASE — VARIANT A USES BACON LARDONS + OLIVE OIL; VARIANT B USES BUTTER: this is a real divergence between the variants, not a preference axis. Julia's variant A renders bacon lardons in olive oil as the fat foundation (traditional bourguignon). Variant B uses BUTTER as the main fat (with olive oil supporting) — the butter enriches the mushroom sauté and gives the sauce body without needing bacon. The butter base is what makes variant B VEGETARIAN when using vegan meat (bacon would make it non-vegetarian). Don't add bacon to variant B; don't skip bacon in variant A (it's Julia's canonical).

RED CHILI FLAKES: a real ingredient in this dish, not a topping. The chili flakes pair particularly well with the tomato + worcestershire (or tamarind paste) axis — they activate the tang and amplify the depth. Without them the dish reads slightly flatter against the same ingredient set. Stir into the simmer; don't sprinkle at the end.

HOT SAUCE (CHOLULA) — SECOND HEAT SOURCE ALONGSIDE THE CHILI FLAKES: a splash of cholula (or similar hot sauce — cholula is the preferred pick, same as in chicken-with-vinegar) works alongside the red chili flakes as an additional source of heat and vinegar-tang. Stir into the simmer with the chili flakes; the two together give a more layered heat than either alone.

=== BALANCE FROM A MIX — NOT FROM ONE SAVORY HEADLINER ===

Stews like this require a lot of balance rather than a single dominant savory source. Satisfying savory comes from a MIX of controlled amounts, not from cranking any one dial:
- SMALL AMOUNTS OF GARLIC
- SMALL TOMATO PASTE
- CONTROLLED BEEF STOCK (or bouillon)
- CONTROLLED NUTRITIONAL YEAST (secondary — see below)
- PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER (secondary — see below)
Each ingredient contributes some savory depth in a slightly different register; over-doing any single one throws the balance off and starts to dominate rather than support. This is different from a dish like chile-colorado or american-chili where one flavor (chile powder, tomato) can lead — here the whole point is a layered supporting stack.

NUTRITIONAL YEAST (SECONDARY) — adds cheesy-adjacent savory depth to the vegan version specifically. Small amount stirred into the simmer. Standard 'part of a broader stack' application — it's fine here because it sits inside a rich, technique-driven flavor architecture rather than doing the umami job alone.

PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER (SECONDARY) — adds concentrated woodsy mushroom depth that reinforces the fresh mushrooms without over-crowding the mushroom axis. Small amount stirred into the simmer.

IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND BEEF — COOK AS MEATBALLS, NOT CRUMBLES: if using impossible meat, beyond beef, or similar extruded plant-based ground beef, form it into MEATBALLS before adding to the stew. Don't break it into crumbles. The extruded proteins in these products recombine during baking — crumbles turn back into a monolithic slab of pseudo-meat in the pot. Pre-formed meatballs hold their shape, and the dish ends up with discrete chunks instead of one giant brick. This is unique to the soy-based products; real ground beef and abbott's-style products don't behave this way.

PRE-BAKE THE MEATBALLS BEFORE ADDING TO THE STEW: bake the formed impossible/beyond meatballs briefly at 350°F first — NOT until fully cooked, just until they firm up on the outside so they hold shape and don't dissolve into the braise. Skip this step and the meatballs risk melting or falling apart in the wet simmer even though they were pre-formed. The pre-bake gives them a slight surface set that survives the stew cook.

=== FRIDGE-AGING BEHAVIOR — BEEF STEW'S MAIN ADVANTAGE ===

One of the big draws of beef stew is that it ages well in the fridge. Not all meat options preserve this:

- IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND BEEF: tastes good in the stew day-of, but causes the stew to AGE MORE POORLY in the fridge. Loses one of beef stew's main advantages.
- GROUND VEGAN BEEF (ABBOTT'S / SOY BEEF CRUMBLES): SAFER for fridge aging than impossible/beyond.
- REAL BEEF or JUST VEGGIES (no meat analog at all): I think this is how to get something properly fridge-friendly.

If you're planning to eat the stew across multiple days, skip impossible/beyond and go with real beef, abbott's-style, or veggies-only.

=== DOESN'T WORK IN A POT PIE (UNLIKE THE CHICKEN VARIANT) ===

This stew never works well in a pot pie, unlike julia child's master chicken stew that lives here as rosemary-chicken-pot-pie. The chicken variants have some specific advantages that this beef-and-mushroom version lacks:

- PEAS PAIR WELL WITH CHICKEN, WHICH WORKS IN PIE FORM: chicken pot pie takes peas as a canonical addition, and peas hold up cleanly inside a pastry crust. Peas don't have the same natural pairing with beef + mushroom + tomato paste, so the pie loses one of its structural components.
- CHICKEN SHREDS CLEANLY; VEGAN/IMPOSSIBLE BEEF (AND PROBABLY REAL BEEF) CLUMPS: shredded chicken distributes evenly through a pie filling. Ground vegan beef or impossible-beef meatballs clump into discrete chunks — reads wrong under a pastry lid, where you want the filling to be a cohesive gravy-bound mixture. Real beef chunks would probably have the same clumping issue.
- POTATOES ARE OPTIONAL IN CHICKEN POT PIE (MIXED EFFECTS IN PIE FORM): the chicken variant doesn't NEED potatoes and often reads better without them (see rosemary-chicken-pot-pie). Potatoes in a pie can absorb too much gravy and leave the filling dry. This stew, on the other hand, has potatoes as a load-bearing structural component (see POTATOES ARE CRITICAL note above) — you can't take them out for the pie format, and leaving them in creates the pie-gravy-absorption problem.

Net: the format tradeoffs stack against the beef version specifically. Keep this stew as a stew.

IF YOU DO WANT A HEARTY BEEF-FLAVORED / DARK PIE, LOOK ELSEWHERE:
- lentil-wellington (Nisha Vora's lentil-mushroom log in puff pastry) is the better option for the hearty-beefy-dark-pastry format — it's built from the ground up for the pie/pastry container and the meat-analog umami stack (walnuts + mushrooms + miso + nutritional yeast + tomato paste) reads correct under pastry the way this stew doesn't.
- atk-vegetable-pot-pie (STUB — unattempted): America's Test Kitchen's veggie pot pie with dark vegetable broth and turnips. Not yet captured or tested in this cookbook — placeholder file exists. The dark-broth-and-turnips approach seems designed for the pie format specifically. Reach for this next time the 'hearty pie' craving hits.

=== BEST PAIRING — HOMEMADE FRENCH ROLLS ===

The best pairing for this stew is homemade french rolls (see artisan-french-bread — bake as rolls rather than a loaf). The rolls do the sauce-sopping job that a pastry lid would in a pot pie format — but external to the dish, which sidesteps all the clumping/potato-absorption problems noted above. A crusty roll torn into the stew or used to soak the gravy on the plate is the intended eating experience for this recipe.
why_i_like_this_recipe: It's the best hearty stew. It doesn't need to be in a pie (like julia child's chicken pie). It allows you to enjoy the components individually when they are on your plate (potato, carrot, mushroom and meat), but the broth is so good, you want to drink it anyway. It stays good in the fridge for days. It requires no blender or huge spice list.
